title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
web_title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Chapter 6: Following the Cash — 10-Year Forensics, ROCE & Balance Sheet Fortress
question: Does Divi's 10-year financial record confirm genuine cash compounding, high return on capital, and clean earnings quality—or are there hidden working-capital or capex cracks?

epigraph.quote: Net profit is an opinion; ten-year cumulative Operating Cash Flow minus cumulative Capex on a debt-free balance sheet is a fact.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Maxim

web_blocks.html: A 10-year audit of Divi's (FY15–FY26 plus Sep 2026 TTM) shows one of the cleanest compounding records in Indian industry. Sales grew 3.39x from ₹3,115 Cr in FY15 to ₹10,560 Cr in FY26, and reached ₹12,191 Cr TTM [1]. Net Profit grew 3.01x from ₹852 Cr to ₹2,568 Cr, and ₹3,363 Cr TTM [1]. Share capital stayed flat at ₹53 Cr since the FY16 bonus issue, with zero dilution over a decade [1].

The P&L history shows clear cycles around a rising margin floor. Operating margin (OPM) never fell below 28% even in the FY24 post-COVID trough [1]. It peaked at 43% in FY22 and again in Q2 FY27 [1]. Depreciation rose from ₹136 Cr (FY15) to ₹463 Cr (FY26) and ₹513 Cr (TTM) as Divi's tripled fixed assets [1]. Even so, PBT margins held 32% in FY26 and 36% TTM, aided by ₹433 Cr of treasury income and just ₹24 Cr of interest [1].

The balance sheet is a debt-free fortress. On September 30, 2026, total debt was just ₹6 Cr against ₹17,997 Cr of equity (Capital ₹53 Cr + Reserves ₹17,944 Cr) [1]. That equals a Debt-to-Equity ratio of 0.0003x [1]. Cash and equivalents stood at ₹2,181 Cr [10]. Fixed Assets plus CWIP grew from ₹1,527 Cr in FY15 to ₹8,641 Cr in FY26 and ₹9,111 Cr by Sep 2026 [1]. Retained earnings funded 100% of that buildout while still paying 24%–50% of profits as dividends [1].

Cash conversion passes forensic checks with ease. From FY15 through FY26, Divi's generated ₹18,356 Cr in cumulative Operating Cash Flow (CFO) against ₹18,976 Cr in Net Profit [1]. That is a 96.7% 12-year CFO-to-PAT ratio, even while funding inventory for a 3.4x larger sales base [1]. Pre-tax CFO/EBITDA averaged 90% over 12 years (105% in FY26, 83% in FY25, 124% in FY23) [1]. Free Cash Flow dipped to ₹215–258 Cr/year in FY24–FY26 only because Investing Cash Flow spent ₹804 Cr (FY25) and ₹2,219 Cr (FY26) on Unit III and peptide lines [1].

Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) fell from its 29%–36% norm (FY15–FY22) to 16% in FY24 as idle new plants weighed on asset turns [1]. It then rebounded to 20% in FY25 and 22% in FY26, with further gains on TTM earnings [1]. Even at the 16% trough, ROCE stayed well above Indian cost of capital (~11%–12%). The main watchpoint is the Cash Conversion Cycle (343 days in FY26), driven by 346 Inventory Days and 103 Debtor Days [1]. Management must keep that strategic stock turning without obsolescence write-offs.

web_blocks.title: Capital Allocation, Dividend Sustainability & Working-Capital Discipline

web_blocks.html: Finally, Divi's balances growth spending with steady shareholder payouts. From FY15 to FY26, dividend payout held at 24%–50% (31% in FY26 at ₹30/share, 36% in FY25, and 50% in FY24) [1][17]. It paid those dividends while self-funding ₹2,219 Cr of investing outflows in FY26 [1]. Unlike weak peers that borrow to pay dividends, Divi's ended Sep 2026 with ₹2,181 Cr in cash and just ₹6 Cr in debt [1][10]. The firm needs zero outside capital to finish Unit III and its peptide lines. Asset quality is equally clean: Divi's carries no acquisition goodwill, pays a full ~24.2% corporate tax rate, and avoids related-party leaks [1]. Every rupee of reported profit sits visibly in tangible plant steel, strategic inventory, or cash reserves.

book_paragraphs: Numbers can tell two stories: the story management wants you to hear on an earnings call, and the story hidden in ten years of audited cash flows. When you and I lay out Divi's Laboratories from FY15 through FY26 and September 2026, what stands out is how little accounting drama there is.

Over that eleven-year span, revenue more than tripled from ₹3,115 crore to ₹10,560 crore in FY26—and reached ₹12,191 crore trailing twelve months by September 2026. Net profit grew from ₹852 crore to ₹2,568 crore in FY26 and ₹3,363 crore trailing twelve months. Share count? Unchanged since FY16. Debt? Effectively zero—just ₹6 crore of borrowings sitting next to ₹17,997 crore of equity and ₹2,181 crore of cash.

book_subsections.title: Forensic Check: Cash Conversion, Capex Intensity, and ROCE
paragraphs: Let's run our toughest forensic test: does accounting profit actually turn into cash? Add up all the Net Profit Divi's reported from FY15 through FY26, and you get ₹18,976 crore. Add up all the Operating Cash Flow it collected over those exact twelve years, and you get ₹18,356 crore—a 96.7% conversion rate, with 106.6% conversion in FY26 alone. That tells us there are no phantom revenues or aggressive channel-stuffing games.

Why, then, did Free Cash Flow look modest at ₹221 crore in FY26? Because Divi's is in the middle of a massive organic buildout—spending over ₹2,200 crore on Unit III in Kakinada and new peptide synthesis lines. Notice what happened to Return on Capital Employed: it dropped to 16% at the FY24 trough while new plants sat under construction, then bounced back to 20% in FY25 and 22% in FY26 as those assets started producing. As long as Inventory Days stay near 346 without write-downs and CWIP continues converting into high-margin Custom Synthesis revenue, the balance sheet remains one of the safest industrial fortresses in India.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: Price-blind underwriting ends right here—and the verdict on business quality is clear. Divi's is a genuine Compounder: zero debt, ~97% decade-long CFO-to-PAT conversion, 22%+ rebounding ROCE, and irreplaceable Big Pharma switching costs. Whether it is an attractive investment depends entirely on what the market is charging for that quality—which we will test next.

book_subsections.title: Dividend Resilience Without Debt: The Ultimate Forensic Proof
paragraphs: One of my favorite forensic checks on any Indian manufacturer is to look at what happens to the dividend during an earnings trough and a heavy capex cycle. Weak companies either slash their dividend to zero or borrow short-term working capital to keep paying shareholders. Look at Divi's during FY24—its toughest post-COVID year, when Net Profit fell to ₹1,600 crore and ROCE dipped to 16%. Divi's paid out 50% of its earnings in dividends, kept borrowings at ₹3 crore, and still funded ₹778 crore of Capital Work-in-Progress for Unit III.

By FY26, as profits recovered to ₹2,568 crore and Operating Cash Flow reached ₹2,738 crore, the payout ratio normalized to 31% while Investing Cash Flow absorbed ₹2,219 crore—leaving ₹2,181 crore of cash on hand by September 2026. Over a full twelve-year cycle, Divi's has proven that its reported earnings are real cash, its capex is self-funded, and its balance sheet is built to survive both industry recessions and regulatory shocks. That completes our price-blind underwriting: the business quality is unequivocally high.
